Reproducing Tian et al. (2025), Figure 4, from dandiset 001559¶

Paper. Tian X, Zhang Y, Du H, Huang W, Bizimana LA, Nishimura N, Ai H (2025). An Enhanced Red Bioluminescent Indicator for Responsive Detection of Physiological Calcium Dynamics in Cells and Mice. ACS Sensors 10(8), 5826-5833. doi:10.1021/acssensors.5c01093. The claims file was written from the version of record (open access, Europe PMC PMC12351538): main text, Methods, legends and Discussion. The Supporting Information was not in that text; it holds nothing on Figure 4.

Dataset. DANDI:001559, version 0.250902.2058. The paper cites no version of the dandiset (it does not name the dandiset at all; the dandiset names the paper). This is the only published version and so the most recent one. The draft has the same 35 assets and the same size (29.39 GB); it was last modified at publication time, so the two do not differ in anything the analysis uses (the archive's list of versions is printed in the data check).

What the dandiset holds, as found below: one mouse (sub-582364L) and only image series. Its description says it holds "all the raw data presented in Figure 4 of the paper, including the python scripts used for analysis and for figure generation"; the raw data of Figure 4 are there (for the one mouse of Figure 4D), the scripts are not. There are no stimulus tables: the stimulus times come from a marker recorded as image channel 1, and nothing says which recording used which electrode or current. Every other figure of the paper (in vitro, cells, neurons, the BLA experiment of Figure 5) is outside the dandiset.

Claim Tested here
fig4b-expression-healthy tested
fig4c-speckle-responsive-region blocked, metadata insufficient (no stimulus times for the speckle movies); the whole time course is described
fig4d-steady-baseline tested
fig4d-evoked-increase tested; the readings of the criterion disagree
fig4d-4ma-single-trials tested, but depends on fig4d-evoked-increase
fig4d-electrode-timing tested, but depends on fig4d-evoked-increase
fig5-bla-footshock-increase, fig5-brep-minimal, fig5-10hz-imaging, fig5-double-bric blocked, data missing (Figure 5 is not in the dandiset)
fig1a-lysate-18fold, fig1b-mutations, fig1d-purified-response, fig1e-kd, lysate-brightness blocked, data missing
fig2b-hela-5fold, fig2c-hek-3p5fold, fig3-neurons-7p3fold, cell-brightness, hek-spectrum, table-s1-fold-gains blocked, data missing

The outcomes, with the reasons, are in the attempt record, attempts/001559-tian-2025-01.yaml.

version 0.250902.2058: 35 assets, 29.39 GB, created 2025-09-02 20:58:29, modified 2025-09-02 20:58:31 UTC
Published 2025-09-02T20:58:29.286613+00:00; summary of version 0.250902.2058: 1 subject(s), 35 files, 29.39 GB

All 35 files are from one mouse, sub-582364L. The paper used six mice for this experiment (Methods, "C57BL/6J mice (n = 6)") and shows one representative mouse in Figure 4D, so the dandiset holds one of the six. The archive's summary of the version says one subject (printed above), which matches.

Every file is a TwoPhotonSeries with unit "n.a.", indicator and location "unknown" and no emission wavelength, and every session description is empty. Three kinds of recording are there, by day: three 40 Hz camera movies on 2025-04-07; six four-channel ScanImage acquisitions on 2025-05-31 (1000 frames of 512 by 512 pixels at 4.228 frames/s, about 236 s each); and two four-channel ScanImage stacks on 2025-06-09. Nothing in the files says what each is; the checks below identify them from the data.

The stated pixel size, 0.028 or 0.014 micrometres, gives a field of 14.4 micrometres, about one neuron. The 2025-06-09 stack of cells (shown under fig4b-expression-healthy) holds about a hundred or more cell bodies in its field, and the wide-field stack shows a whole branching vessel tree, so the stated pixel size is wrong (likely a unit or scale error). No spatial measure below uses it.

# The ScanImage series give either a rate or a timestamp array; check that the timestamps are regular.
rows = []
for a in ebric.assets():
    if "20250531" not in a.path and "20250609" not in a.path:
        continue
    f = ebric.open_asset(a)
    name = list(f["acquisition"])[0]
    s = f["acquisition"][name]
    if "timestamps" in s:
        ts = s["timestamps"][:]
        d = np.diff(ts)
        rows.append({"session": ebric.session_of(a.path), "series": name, "n": len(ts), "first": ts[0],
                     "dt_min": d.min(), "dt_max": d.max(), "dt_median": np.median(d)})
ts_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(ts_tab.groupby("session").agg(files=("series", "size"), n=("n", "first"), first=("first", "first"),

Where a file has timestamps they start at 0 and are regular, with intervals equal to the inverse of the rate the other files state for the same kind of acquisition (0.2365 s, 4.228 frames/s, on 2025-05-31). So frame times are frame index over rate in every file of that day. The four channels of an acquisition are four files with the same session start time and the same frames, so they share one clock by construction.

Every file has the same top-level groups. In each, acquisition holds one image series; stimulus holds only empty presentation and templates groups; processing and analysis are empty; and no file has an intervals group. So no file holds stimulus times, trial intervals or processed data, as the archive's asset metadata also says.

Channel 1 is a stimulus marker: it sits at about -580 and drops to about -1990 in pulses. Its value is the same on every line of a frame (the spread within a frame is printed), so it is the frame's average of the marker, and the frames in which a pulse starts or ends lie between the two levels, at most two per pulse. Placing each edge within its frame by that value (ebric.marker_onsets) gives pulses of 4.985 to 4.992 s in every session. The Methods give trains of 5 s ("Electrical stimulation (5 Hz, 5 s, 2 mA and 4 mA)"), so the pulses are read as the stimulation periods; the files do not say so. The first two sessions (14:42 and 14:46) have no pulses, the other four have 8, 8, 7 and 10, at irregular intervals of 12.2 to 56.6 s. Nothing in the files says which of the two electrodes or which current (2 or 4 mA) each session or trial used.

# Which channels carry the bioluminescence, and do the stimulus markers share their clock?
# Contrast: mean response (0 to 5 s after onset minus the 5 s before) at the true onsets against
# the same onsets moved together by a random circular shift (1000 shifts per session).
rng_seed = 11
rows = []
for s in stim_sessions:
    for c in (2, 3, 4):
        t, x = ebric.binned(pmt[s][c])
        true = ebric.trial_table(t, x, onsets[s])["resp_a"].mean()
        null = ebric.shifted_null(t, x, onsets[s], n=1000, seed=rng_seed)
        rows.append({"session": s, "channel": c, "true": true, "null_mean": null.mean(), "null_sd": null.std(),
                     "z": (true - null.mean()) / null.std(), "p_shift": (np.sum(null >= true) + 1) / (len(null) + 1)})
clock = pd.DataFrame(rows)

Channels 3 and 4 increase after the marker onsets, far beyond the shifted onsets in the two middle sessions (z above 5) and less so in the first and last (z 1.7 to 2.9); channel 2 changes by about a tenth as much in the two middle sessions and not in the others, as a channel that passes a little of the red light would. So the marker and the bioluminescence share a clock, consistent with their being channels of one acquisition. The sizes per session are the subject of fig4d-evoked-increase.

Each panel is clipped to its 1st and 99.5th percentiles (printed in its title); 1.5% of pixels lie outside.

In the wide-field stack (14:22) channel 2 shows the vessels bright, as FITC-dextran labels them (Figure 4B legend, "Blood vessels were labeled with FITC-dextran (green)"); channel 4 shows a bright region with the vessels dark, and its pixels are anticorrelated with channel 2; channel 3 shows both the bright region and the vessels, and is positively correlated with channel 2. Channel 4 is therefore the channel that sees the red eBRIC emission without the green dye, as a 645/65 filter would (Methods, "a 645/65 filter on photomultiplier tube"); channel 3 passes some green as well. This identifies channel 4 as the 645/65 channel, consistent with the data but not stated in them; the analyses use channel 4 and show channel 3 as a variant. The frame means of both stacks rise and fall over the frames, consistent with z-stacks through the tissue. Channel 1 holds only scan noise.

The three movies of 2025-04-07 are labelled as two-photon imaging, but they are 40 Hz camera movies whose frames cycle through four exposure levels (the frame mean takes four values in turn, with little spread within each), and their speckle contrast maps show the vessel tree. This is consistent with multi-exposure laser speckle imaging (the paper cites Rivera and Schaffer's multi-exposure speckle method), that is, the speckle data of Figure 4C. They carry no stimulus marker, no description and no times of stimulation.

fig4b-expression-healthy¶

Two-photon fluorescence shows robust eBRIC expression in neuronal somata and processes in the whisker barrel cortex, and the neurons look healthy and intact three months after surgery.

Criterion: reproduced when the two-photon fluorescence images show labelled cell bodies and processes in the transduced region; the date relative to surgery is reported from the metadata if given; health is not judged.

Result: reproduced. The channel 4 stack of 2025-06-09 shows bright, compact, cell-sized objects (184 at sigma 4 px and 91 at sigma 6 px, their centres a median 1.70 and 2.03 times the local median) in labelled tissue whose median is 3.55 times the darkest 5% of the field (the vessel shadows), and in the wide-field stack the brightest 5% of pixels lie above 519 units against a median of 17, a bounded bright region under the window. The cell-sized objects are labelled somata; processes are not resolved one by one, and the labelling between the somata (the neuropil) is the form they take at this resolution, judged from the image. The files give no surgery date: the stacks were taken 63 days after the first recording through the window, so at least two months after surgery, consistent with but not showing the paper's three months.

fig4c-speckle-responsive-region¶

Laser speckle contrast imaging shows that the region of viral expression responds with blood flow changes to electrical stimulation of the whisker pad.

Blocked. The speckle movies are present (checked above), but they carry no stimulus times or marker, and nothing in the dandiset records when the whisker pad was stimulated during them, so "during stimulation compared with before it" cannot be formed from the data. Finding the stimulation periods from the flow signal itself would assume the response the claim tests.

The cell below describes the speckle contrast over every frame of the three movies, as a partial look and not a test: with no stimulus times it cannot compare stimulation with the time before it, and since the registration of the speckle field to the eBRIC region is not recorded, it uses the whole field and regions of 40 by 40 pixels. It reports how large the changes of the flow index are and whether they come in episodes.

In [15]:
# Partial look, not a test: the speckle contrast over every frame of the three movies, with no
# stimulus times to compare against. Block contrast K in 8 x 8 pixels, averaged over regions of
# 40 x 40 pixels; flow index 1/K^2 per exposure phase (frame index mod 4, so 10 Hz per phase),
# whole field, relative to its median.
t0 = time.time()
spk_full = {}
for a in apr:
    spk_full[ebric.session_of(a.path)] = ebric.speckle_timecourse(a)
print(f"read every frame of the {len(spk_full)} movies in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
rows, traces = [], {}
for s, (R, Km, rate) in spk_full.items():
    for p in range(4):
        F = 1 / R[p::4] ** 2
        fw = F.reshape(len(F), -1).mean(1)
        rel = fw / np.median(fw) - 1
        fs = rate / 4
        sm = ndimage.uniform_filter1d(rel, int(fs))                      # 1 s moving average
        dev = sm - ndimage.median_filter(sm, int(30 * fs) + 1, mode="nearest")   # minus a 30 s running median
        mad = 1.4826 * np.median(np.abs(dev - np.median(dev)))
        pk, _ = signal.find_peaks(dev, height=3 * mad, distance=int(2 * fs))
        f_, P = signal.welch(rel - rel.mean(), fs=fs, nperseg=int(60 * fs))
        band = (f_ > 0.03) & (f_ < 0.5)
        traces[(s, p)] = (np.arange(len(rel)) / fs, sm)
        rows.append({"movie": s, "phase": p, "mean K": float(Km[p].mean()), "frames": len(rel),
                     "rel. flow s.d.": rel.std(), "1 s smoothed range": f"{sm.min():.3f} to {sm.max():.3f}",
                     "robust s.d. of fluctuation": mad, "episodes > 3 robust s.d.": len(pk),
                     "episode heights": np.round(dev[pk], 3).tolist(), "episode times (s)": np.round(pk / fs, 1).tolist(),
                     "spectral peak period 2-33 s (s)": 1 / f_[band][np.argmax(P[band])]})
spk_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(spk_tab.round(4).to_string(index=False))
# Is the fluctuation local? Share of each region's (1 s smoothed, detrended) variance explained by the whole field.
for s, (R, Km, rate) in spk_full.items():
    p = 2
    F = 1 / R[p::4] ** 2
    F = F / np.median(F, axis=0) - 1
    fs = rate / 4
    sm = ndimage.uniform_filter1d(F, int(fs), axis=0)
    sm = sm - ndimage.median_filter(sm, size=(int(30 * fs) + 1, 1, 1), mode="nearest")
    w = sm.reshape(len(sm), -1)
    whole = w.mean(1)
    r2 = np.array([np.corrcoef(whole, w[:, i])[0, 1] ** 2 for i in range(w.shape[1])])
    amp = w.std(0)
    print(f"{s} phase {p}: region fluctuation s.d. median {np.median(amp):.4f} (range {amp.min():.4f} to {amp.max():.4f}); "
          f"variance shared with the whole field, median {np.median(r2):.2f} (range {r2.min():.2f} to {r2.max():.2f})")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(15, 9))
for a_, s in zip(ax, spk_full):
    for p in range(4):
        tt, sm = traces[(s, p)]
        a_.plot(tt, sm, lw=0.7, label=f"phase {p}")
    a_.set_title(f"{s}: whole-field flow index 1/K^2, relative to median, 1 s smoothed", fontsize=9)
    a_.set_xlabel("time in movie (s)")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Every trace is drawn in full; ranges are in the table above.")

Result: blocked, metadata insufficient. Over every frame of the three movies, the whole-field flow index (1/K^2 relative to its median) has an s.d. of 0.8% to 4.5% in exposure phases 1 to 3 and 5.9% to 11.3% in phase 0, the noisiest. Departures of the 1 s smoothed index from its 30 s running median pass 3 robust s.d. at most three times per movie in phases 1 to 3: once in 12:23 (phase 1, 1.1% at 105.4 s), never in 12:37, and three times in 12:49 (0.9% to 2.6%; at 27.5, 60.3 and 99.6 s in phase 1, and at about 27.5, 41.6 and 99.6 s in phases 2 and 3). The spectrum between 2 and 33 s peaks at its longest period (30 s) in phases 1 to 3 of every movie except phase 1 of 12:49 (4.6 s). The regions share a median of 6% to 12% of their fluctuation variance with the whole field (phase 2). So the flow index shows slow drift and a few small episodes, without a repeated change at a regular period. Whether any of it is a response to stimulation cannot be told without the stimulus times.

Conditions of the stimulated sessions¶

The four stimulated sessions are taken to be the four conditions of Figure 4D (two electrodes by two currents), one condition per session: the paper reports exactly four, the dandiset holds the raw data of Figure 4 for one mouse, and each session holds one series of 7 to 10 trials. Which session is which is not recorded. The criteria of the dependent claims need the current; the paper says the 4 mA condition gives the response strong enough for single events, so the assumption adopted is that the two sessions with the larger mean response are the 4 mA ones. Every other pairing is shown where a result depends on it.

In [16]:
CH = 4   # channel 4 is the 645/65 channel (data check); channel 3 is shown as a variant
trials = {}
for s in stim_sessions:
    for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:

The trial responses show no sign of two conditions alternating or in blocks within a session: odd and even trials, and the first and second halves, do not differ (Mann-Whitney p 0.31 to 0.89). Every trial of the two strong sessions is 7.64 or more; of the 18 trials of the two weak sessions, one (7.77, the first of 14:50) is above that. This is consistent with one current per session but does not show it. In 15:04, five trials lie at -2.0 to -0.3 and five at 2.9 to 7.5, which a mix of two electrodes or failures of response could both give. Which electrode each session used cannot be told from the data.

fig4d-steady-baseline¶

Infusing DTZ at 25 uL/min through the tail vein gives a steady level of baseline bioluminescence during the recording.

Criterion: per recording, the baseline of each trial (mean of the 5 s before onset); reproduced when the baseline changes from the first to the last trial by less than the mean 4 mA evoked response. The criterion compares with the 4 mA response "in the same recording"; here a recording holds one condition, so the 2 mA recordings have no 4 mA response of their own. The comparison is made with the mean 4 mA response of the same channel (the two assumed 4 mA sessions), in both response windows; the recording's own response is shown as a variant.

# Variant: a straight-line trend in place of the first-to-last difference, over the trial baselines
# and over every bin outside the 0 to 15 s after each onset.
rows = []
for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
    ref = {k: np.mean([trials[(s, c)][f"resp_{k}"].mean() for s in four_ma]) for k in "ab"}
    for s in stim_sessions:
        tb = trials[(s, c)]
        t, x = ebric.binned(pmt[s][c])
        quiet = np.ones(t.size, bool)
        for t0 in onsets[s]:
            quiet &= ~((t >= t0) & (t < t0 + 15))
        tr_b = np.polyfit(tb.onset_s, tb.baseline, 1)[0] * (tb.onset_s.iloc[-1] - tb.onset_s.iloc[0])
        tr_q = np.polyfit(t[quiet], x[quiet], 1)[0] * (t[-1] - t[0])
        rows.append({"channel": c, "session": s[9:], "trend of trial baselines, first to last onset": tr_b,
                     "trend of bins outside responses, whole recording": tr_q,
                     "4 mA mean resp a": ref["a"], "4 mA mean resp b": ref["b"],
                     "both trends < 4 mA a": max(abs(tr_b), abs(tr_q)) < ref["a"],
                     "both trends < 4 mA b": max(abs(tr_b), abs(tr_q)) < ref["b"]})
print("\nLinear trends (units over the span):")

Result: partially reproduced, resting on the assumed 4 mA sessions. In three of the four stimulated recordings the baseline changes from the first to the last trial by less than the mean 4 mA response (at most 6.64 against 13.60 or more), in both channels and both windows. In the first stimulated recording (14:50) the channel 4 baseline rises by 18.34 units (channel 3 by 17.53), more than the mean 4 mA response in either window (17.44 and 14.13), so there the responses do not stand out from the drift by this criterion. The channel 4 level also rises within the two unstimulated sessions before it (by 6.39 and 11.02) and from about 352 to about 402 over the day. With the 4 mA reference taken from the two weak sessions (2.49 or 2.02), the 14:55 recording fails as well. With a straight-line trend in place of the first-to-last difference, the 14:50 recording still fails in channel 4 (16.11 over the trial baselines and 18.00 over all bins outside the responses, against 17.44 and 14.13); in channel 3 its trends (15.18 and 15.08) lie below the window a reference (16.61) and above the window b one (13.60). The 14:55 trend over its whole recording, 13.83, is close to the window b reference of 14.13; the other two recordings stay well below. The rise of about 50 units over the six recordings of the day is larger than the mean 4 mA response; the criterion judges each recording, so it does not enter the outcome, but the level is not steady across the recordings.

fig4d-evoked-increase¶

Whisker pad stimulation (5 Hz for 5 s) at 4 mA and at 2 mA, through each of the two electrodes, gives clear increases in cortical eBRIC bioluminescence.

Criterion: per condition, the trial responses (mean in the response window minus the mean of the 5 s before onset) tested one-sided against zero, with windows (a) 0 to 5 s and (b) 0 to 10 s and tests (1) Wilcoxon signed-rank and (2) one-sample t-test; an increase when the mean is positive and p < 0.05; reproduced when all four conditions show an increase, the outcome being the one all windows and tests give, and methods_underspecified when they differ. One mouse is in the dandiset, so both readings of which mice are the same. With one condition per session, the result does not depend on which session is which condition. That each session holds one condition is itself an assumption (the trial order is checked above, but cannot show it): if a session, 15:04 in particular, held trials of two conditions, the per-condition tests would change, and the outcome could change with them.

Result: blocked, methods underspecified. Two sessions respond strongly (channel 4, window a, mean 15.93 and 18.95 units, every trial positive, Wilcoxon p = 0.0039 and 0.0078, t-test p < 0.0001), and in channel 4 the 14:50 session shows a smaller increase (2.65 and 3.03 units) significant under both windows and both tests. The 15:04 session decides the outcome: its mean response is positive in both windows, but it is significant only by the t-test in window a (p = 0.046; Wilcoxon p = 0.116; window b p = 0.246 and 0.211). Channel 3 gives the same split, and there the 14:50 session also fails the Wilcoxon test in window a (p = 0.125). So all four conditions show an increase under one reading of window and test and three of four (two of four in one channel 3 reading) under the others, and the criterion makes the claim methods_underspecified when the readings disagree. This outcome rests on the assumption that each session is one condition: if 15:04, whose trials split into five below zero and five above, held two conditions, the per-condition tests would change, and the outcome could change with them. The 15:04 session's trials come at intervals of 12.2 to 32.1 s, and the baselines of two of them start within 10 s of the previous onset.

fig4d-4ma-single-trials¶

At 4 mA the response is strong enough to detect individual stimulation events, in single trials without averaging.

Criterion: reading (a), single 5 s trials: a trial is detected when its response exceeds k times the s.d. of its 1 s smoothed baseline, k = 2 or 3, in both windows; reproduced when more than half of the 4 mA trials are detected under all of them. Reading (b), single pulses of the 5 Hz train, is shown as a variant on the unsmoothed signal folded on the 0.2 s pulse period. The claim depends on fig4d-evoked-increase.

# Variant (b): single pulses. Unsmoothed bins of 128 lines are too coarse for 0.2 s pulses, so the
# line signal is used (0.46 ms per line), each stimulation segment detrended, folded in 20 phase bins.
# Null: the same fold of the 5 s before each onset.
rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
rows = []
for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
    for s in stim_sessions:
        x, t = pmt[s][c]["lines"].ravel(), pmt[s][c]["t"].ravel()
        prof, per = ebric.pulse_fold(t, x, onsets[s])
        pre, per0 = ebric.pulse_fold(t, x, onsets[s] - ebric.STIM_S)
        p2p, p2p0 = np.ptp(prof), np.ptp(pre)
        # trial-level test of the phase modulation: per-trial peak-to-peak, stimulation against before
        a, b = np.ptp(per, axis=1), np.ptp(per0, axis=1)
        rows.append({"channel": c, "session": s, "fold p2p during": p2p, "fold p2p before": p2p0,
                     "per-trial p2p during (median)": np.median(a), "before (median)": np.median(b),
                     "p (Wilcoxon, during > before)": stats.wilcoxon(a, b, alternative="greater").pvalue,
                     "phase of max (s)": np.argmax(prof) * 0.01})
pulses = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(pulses.round(4).to_string(index=False))

Result: blocked, because fig4d-evoked-increase is blocked (methods underspecified). The test itself ran: under the assumed current, every 4 mA trial in both sessions (15 of 15) exceeds 3 times the s.d. of its smoothed baseline in both windows and both channels, so more than half under every reading. If the 4 mA pair includes one of the weak sessions, the pooled fraction is 0.53 to 0.75, still above half; if it is the two weak sessions, it is 0.28 to 0.50. In channel 4 the single-pulse variant does not show responses to individual pulses: the folded modulation at the 0.2 s period during stimulation is close to that of the 5 s before (0.31 against 0.27 and 0.47 against 0.37 in the two 4 mA sessions), and the per-trial comparison is not significant in any session (p 0.11 to 0.19). In channel 3 it is significant in two sessions, 14:59 (an assumed 4 mA session, p = 0.023) and 14:50 (an assumed 2 mA session, p = 0.039), and not in 14:55 (p = 0.156) or 15:04. So the single-pulse variant does not decide the claim either way. Leaving the last 0.5 s out of the baseline s.d. (its centred 1 s average takes in signal after onset) leaves every 4 mA fraction at 1.0 and gives 2 mA pooled fractions of 0.17 to 0.44.

fig4d-electrode-timing¶

The responses to the two electrode locations differ in timing; stimulation of region 1 gives a delayed peak, and region 2 an earlier rise after stimulation onset.

Criterion: per condition, the trial-averaged trace smoothed with a 1 s moving average, baseline the 5 s before onset; time to peak is the time of the maximum from onset to 10 s; time of rise is the first time after onset above half the peak. The dataset does not label the electrodes, so the claim is tested as one electrode having both the later peak and the later rise, at either current. The claim depends on fig4d-evoked-increase.

In [23]:
rows = []
for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
    for s in stim_sessions:
        t, x = ebric.binned(pmt[s][c])
        g, tr = ebric.event_average(t, x, onsets[s])
        pr = ebric.peak_and_rise(g, tr.mean(0))
        rows.append({"channel": c, "session": s, "assumed current": "4 mA" if s in four_ma else "2 mA",
                     "trials averaged": len(tr), **pr})
timing = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(timing.round(3).to_string(index=False))

def later_both(c, pair):
    a, b = (timing[(timing.channel == c) & (timing.session == s)].iloc[0] for s in pair)
    if a.peak_time_s > b.peak_time_s and a.rise_time_s > b.rise_time_s:
        return pair[0]
    if b.peak_time_s > a.peak_time_s and b.rise_time_s > a.rise_time_s:
        return pair[1]
    return None

print()
for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
    for name, pair in (("4 mA", four_ma), ("2 mA", two_ma)):
        r1 = later_both(c, pair)
        print(f"channel {c}, {name} {[s[9:] for s in pair]}: session with both the later peak and the later rise:",
              r1[9:] if r1 else "none")

# Bootstrap over trials: how often does the same session have both later times?
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
print("\nBootstrap over trials (1000 resamples), fraction of resamples where each session has both later times:")
for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
    for name, pair in (("4 mA", four_ma), ("2 mA", two_ma)):
        avgs = {}
        for s in pair:
            t, x = ebric.binned(pmt[s][c])
            avgs[s] = ebric.event_average(t, x, onsets[s])
        cnt = {pair[0]: 0, pair[1]: 0, None: 0}
        for _ in range(1000):
            pr = {}
            for s in pair:
                g, tr = avgs[s]
                pr[s] = ebric.peak_and_rise(g, tr[rng.integers(0, len(tr), len(tr))].mean(0))
            a, b = pr[pair[0]], pr[pair[1]]
            if a["peak_time_s"] > b["peak_time_s"] and a["rise_time_s"] > b["rise_time_s"]:
                cnt[pair[0]] += 1
            elif b["peak_time_s"] > a["peak_time_s"] and b["rise_time_s"] > a["rise_time_s"]:
                cnt[pair[1]] += 1
            else:
                cnt[None] += 1
        print(f"  channel {c}, {name}: {pair[0][9:]} {cnt[pair[0]] / 1000:.3f}, {pair[1][9:]} {cnt[pair[1]] / 1000:.3f}, neither {cnt[None] / 1000:.3f}")

print("\nUnder every pairing of the sessions into two currents (channel 4):")
for p in pairings:
    q = tuple(s for s in stim_sessions if s not in p)
    res = [later_both(CH, p), later_both(CH, q)]
    print(f"  {[s[9:] for s in p]} / {[s[9:] for s in q]}: later both -> {[r[9:] if r else None for r in res]}")

# The averaged traces around onset, and two variants of the time of rise:
# (ii) the start of the run above half peak that holds the peak, searched from -5 s (smoothed trace);
# (iii) the first time after onset at which the unsmoothed average exceeds half the smoothed peak.
rows = []
for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
    for s in stim_sessions:
        t, x = ebric.binned(pmt[s][c])
        g, tr = ebric.event_average(t, x, onsets[s])
        g_raw, tr_raw = ebric.event_average(t, x, onsets[s], smoothed=False)
        avg, raw = tr.mean(0), tr_raw.mean(0)
        base, base_raw = avg[g < 0].mean(), raw[g_raw < 0].mean()
        pr = ebric.peak_and_rise(g, avg)
        pc = ebric.peak_and_rise(g, avg, rise="crossing")
        above = np.where((g_raw >= 0) & (raw - base_raw > pr["peak"] / 2))[0]
        rows.append({"channel": c, "session": s, "assumed current": "4 mA" if s in four_ma else "2 mA",
                     "peak_time_s": pr["peak_time_s"], "peak": pr["peak"], "rise (i) first after onset": pr["rise_time_s"],
                     "rise (ii) crossing": pc["rise_time_s"], "rise (iii) unsmoothed": g_raw[above[0]] if above.size else np.nan,
                     "smoothed at onset": np.interp(0, g, avg - base),
                     "smoothed, mean -1 to 0 s": (avg - base)[(g >= -1) & (g < 0)].mean(),
                     "unsmoothed, mean -1 to 0 s": (raw - base_raw)[(g_raw >= -1) & (g_raw < 0)].mean(),
                     "unsmoothed, mean 0 to 0.5 s": (raw - base_raw)[(g_raw >= 0) & (g_raw < 0.5)].mean()})
        if c == CH:
            sel = (g >= -2) & (g <= 3)
            print(f"{s[9:]} channel {c}: baseline {base:.2f}, half peak {pr['peak'] / 2:.2f}; minus baseline, every 4th bin from -2 to 3 s")
            print("   time    ", np.round(g[sel][::4], 2).tolist())
            print("   smoothed", np.round((avg - base)[sel][::4], 2).tolist())
            print("   raw     ", np.round((raw - base_raw)[sel][::4], 2).tolist())
rise_var = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(rise_var.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print()
for col in ("rise (i) first after onset", "rise (ii) crossing", "rise (iii) unsmoothed"):
    for c in ebric.BL_CHANNELS:
        for name, pair in (("4 mA", four_ma), ("2 mA", two_ma)):
            a, b = (rise_var[(rise_var.channel == c) & (rise_var.session == s)].iloc[0] for s in pair)
            later = (pair[0] if a.peak_time_s > b.peak_time_s and a[col] > b[col] else
                     pair[1] if b.peak_time_s > a.peak_time_s and b[col] > a[col] else None)
            print(f"{col}, channel {c}, {name}: session with both later -> {later[9:] if later else 'none'}")

rise (iii) unsmoothed, channel 4, 4 mA: session with both later -> none
rise (iii) unsmoothed, channel 4, 2 mA: session with both later -> 145053

Result: blocked, because fig4d-evoked-increase is blocked (methods underspecified). The test itself ran. At the assumed 2 mA the 14:50 session has both the later peak and the later rise in both channels (channel 4, peak 4.42 against 3.60 s, rise 2.54 against 0.005 s), in 0.89 to 0.98 of bootstrap resamples; but the 15:04 average there is small (peak 2.54 units) and crosses half its peak at onset. At the assumed 4 mA neither session has both later times: in channel 4 the peaks fall in the same 59 ms bin (3.71 s), and in channel 3 the later peak goes with the earlier rise. So the criterion's condition holds at one current, the weaker one, under the assumed pairing; under the other pairings of sessions into currents some session also has both later times at one current (printed above).

Around onset, the smoothed 15:04 average is already 1.69 above its baseline at onset, against a half peak of 1.27. Its unsmoothed average is 0.77 above baseline in the second before onset and jumps above half the peak in the first bin after onset (mean 2.54 over 0 to 0.5 s), so the early rise is a step at onset with a smaller elevation before it, which the centred 1 s average moves earlier. With the rise taken as the start of the run above half peak (-0.23 s for 15:04, 2.54 s for 14:50) or from the unsmoothed average (0.005 and 2.36 s), 14:50 still has both later times at the assumed 2 mA in both channels, and neither 4 mA session does.

Claims outside Figure 4¶

The dandiset holds the in vivo cortical recordings of Figure 4 only. The in vitro and cell data of Figures 1 to 3 and S1 to S3, Table S1, and the awake BLA imaging of Figure 5 are not in it, and the paper deposits no data elsewhere (its data statement names only the Addgene plasmids). These claims are blocked, data missing: fig1a-lysate-18fold, fig1b-mutations, fig1d-purified-response, fig1e-kd, lysate-brightness, fig2b-hela-5fold, fig2c-hek-3p5fold, fig3-neurons-7p3fold, cell-brightness, hek-spectrum, table-s1-fold-gains, fig5-bla-footshock-increase, fig5-brep-minimal, fig5-10hz-imaging and fig5-double-bric.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The paper gives no response window, baseline, test or detection rule for Figure 4D; those of the claims file's criteria are used, each reading run. The time base is bins of 128 scan lines (59 ms) of the frame signal. Channel 4 is taken as the 645/65 PMT and channel 3 shown as a variant. The four stimulated sessions are taken as the four conditions, and the two with the larger responses as the 4 mA ones, an assumption the data cannot check. One mouse of the paper's six is in the dandiset.

What was found about the dataset. It holds one mouse, as image series only. The stimulus times are recorded only as an undescribed image channel, and no file says which electrode or current a session used, which channel is which detector, or what the 2025-04-07 movies are (labelled two-photon, they are consistent with multi-exposure speckle imaging and carry no stimulus times). No file holds a stimulus table, trial intervals or processed data (every file's groups are listed in the data check). The stated pixel sizes (0.028 and 0.014 micrometres) cannot be right. The analysis scripts named in the description are not in the dandiset.
